deep.reconstruction:
Context (end of §XIII, previous page): Euler's buckling load for a cylindrical column of height a is P = π²·Ekk/a², where Ekk is the 'moment de roideur' (modern flexural rigidity EI). To give a sense of how large this load is, he imagines the same force applied horizontally at the top of the column, clamped at its foot like a cantilever. This is the experiment of §VIII, from which the stiffness is measured. The linear cantilever tip deflection in §VIII is Dδ = F a³/(3Ekk). Substituting F = π²Ekk/a² gives Dδ = (π²/3)·a, and with π² ≈ 10 this is about 3⅓·a = 3⅓·AC. Euler notes this is impossible: the tip of a bar of length a cannot move sideways by more than a. He diagnoses the reason correctly. The formula assumes an infinitesimal (linearized) deflection, and a fully rigorous large-deflection calculation (the elastica) would give a much smaller Dδ. His qualitative point still holds: such a force applied horizontally would produce an enormous bend, so the vertical load a column can carry is very large.

§XIV (programme): Euler will now give a derivation aimed only at columns. His earlier treatment, the 1744 Additamentum 'De curvis elasticis' to the Methodus inveniendi, was framed for elastic laminae and mixed with other questions. A separate derivation should reassure readers that 'la considération du ressort', i.e. the elastic-lamina viewpoint, does not change the deflected curve. He will first treat prismatic columns (constant EI), then columns of variable thickness. He warns that the general variable-section problem 'surpasse les bornes de l'analyse'. In modern terms, the eigenvalue problem (EI(x)y')' + ..., or EI(x)y'' + Py = 0, has no closed-form solution for general EI(x). He will therefore treat only particular cases, which he says will shed light both on the subject and on analysis in general.

§XV (start): a cylindrical column carries a load just large enough to bend it infinitesimally, with deflected shape AMC (Fig. 2). The next page sets up EI·y'' + P y = 0 for the pin-ended column and integrates it.
errors: No mathematical error. Euler himself flags that applying the linear (small-deflection) cantilever formula here is illegitimate.
Only the approximation π² ≈ 10 is used; this is harmless.

The claim that the exact large-deflection value is 'beaucoup plus petit' is correct. For a cantilever with load parameter FL²/EI ≈ 9.87, the nonlinear elastica gives a horizontal tip displacement of roughly 0.8L (approximate value recalled from the nonlinear cantilever literature), against the linear prediction of 3.3L.

ideas.what: Comparing the critical buckling load with the same force applied as a transverse tip load on a cantilever. Linear theory then gives tip deflection π²a/3, which exposes the scale of the buckling load.
ideas.modern_name: Linear cantilever deflection FL³/(3EI) versus Euler critical load; heuristic sizing of P_cr

ideas.what: Explicit recognition that small-deflection theory breaks down for large loads, and that the exact (nonlinear elastica) calculation gives a much smaller deflection.
ideas.modern_name: Limits of linearized beam theory; geometric nonlinearity / large-deflection elastica
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (elastica 1744); large-deflection cantilever analyses in the 20th century (e.g. Bisshopp–Drucker 1945)

ideas.what: Statement that buckling of variable-section columns is not solvable in general, so only special cases are treated.
ideas.modern_name: Variable-coefficient Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem (EI(x)y')' + Py = 0, or EI(x)y'' + Py = 0); for power-law sections, solutions in Bessel functions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E238; later E508–E510, 1778); Lagrange 1770–73 on optimal columns; Clausen 1851
ideas.where_published: E238 later sections; Acta Acad. Petrop. 1778 column papers (E508–E510)

ideas.what: Re-derivation of column buckling independent of the elastic-lamina framework, for a pin-ended prismatic column under infinitesimal deflection.
ideas.modern_name: Euler buckling of pin-ended column via the linearized moment equation

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known paper in the history of elasticity (Truesdell's 1960 volume of the Opera omnia, Ser. II vol. 11.2, discusses it). The page contains a heuristic illustration, a correct remark on the limits of linearization, and a programmatic statement on variable-section columns. All are documented and nothing appears overlooked.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. 'reſtraindrai' is a period spelling for 'restreindrai' and is as printed.
Margin reference 'Fig. 2.' belongs beside §XV, next to 'AMC'.
The page number 259 and signature 'Kk 2' are correct.
